If the unitary time-evolution operator is differentiable in $t$, define the **Hamiltonian**
$$H(t) \equiv i\hbar\, \frac{\partial U(t \leftarrow 0)}{\partial t}\, U^\dagger(t \leftarrow 0) = H^\dagger(t). \tag{69}$$

<span id="prop-66"></span>**Proposition 66.** The density matrix satisfies the von Neumann equation, a rank-one state vector satisfies the Schrödinger equation, expectation values satisfy the Ehrenfest equation, and Heisenberg-picture operators satisfy the Heisenberg equation of motion:
$$i\hbar\, \frac{\partial \rho(t)}{\partial t} = [H(t), \rho(t)], \tag{70}$$
$$i\hbar\, \frac{\partial \Psi(t)}{\partial t} = H(t)\Psi(t), \tag{71}$$
$$\frac{d\langle A(t)\rangle}{dt} = \left\langle \frac{i}{\hbar}[H(t), A(t)] \right\rangle + \left\langle \frac{\partial A(t)}{\partial t} \right\rangle. \tag{72}$$

Thus the Schrödinger equation is *derived*, not postulated, from an indivisible stochastic process with a differentiable unistochastic transition matrix. The conditions of linearity and probability conservation alone are insufficient to pick out unitarity—CPTP maps such as the bit-flip channel are linear and probability-conserving without being unitary—so the derivation of unitarity is a substantive result [@barandes2025quantum].

## 14. Gauge Invariance and Dynamical Symmetries

### 14.1 Foldy–Wouthuysen gauge transformations

<span id="prop-67"></span>**Proposition 67 (Second gauge invariance).** Let $V(t)$ be a time-dependent unitary matrix. The transformation
$$
\begin{aligned}
\rho(t) &\mapsto V(t)\rho(t)V^\dagger(t), \\
\Psi(t) &\mapsto V(t)\Psi(t), \\
A(t) &\mapsto V(t)A(t)V^\dagger(t), \\
\Theta(t \leftarrow 0) &\mapsto V(t)\,\Theta(t \leftarrow 0)\, V^\dagger(0)
\end{aligned} \tag{74}
$$
leaves the probabilities, expectation values, and the transition matrix unchanged [@barandes2025correspondence].

This is a gauge invariance first written down for the Dirac equation by Foldy and Wouthuysen [@foldy1950]. If $V$ is time-independent it is a change of orthonormal basis; if it depends on time it is a local-in-time unitary transformation of each Hilbert-space fiber. Under it, when $\Theta = U$ is unitary, the Hamiltonian transforms as a non-Abelian gauge potential:
$$H(t) \mapsto V(t)H(t)V^\dagger(t) - i\hbar\, V(t)\frac{\partial V^\dagger(t)}{\partial t}. \tag{75}$$
Choosing $V(t) = U^\dagger(t\leftarrow 0)$ makes $H_V = 0$—which is precisely the Heisenberg picture. Consequently the Hamiltonian is not a gauge-invariant observable, and the familiar Hilbert-space ingredients are highly gauge-dependent; one may reasonably be skeptical of assigning them direct ontological meaning [@barandes2025correspondence].

### 14.2 Dynamical symmetries and Noether's theorem

<span id="def-68"></span>**Definition 68 (Dynamical symmetry).** For an invertible transformation of configurations $P_i \mapsto \tilde P_i = V^\dagger P_i V$ (with $V$ unitary), the transformation is a *dynamical symmetry* if it leaves the transition matrix invariant:
$$\operatorname{tr}\!\left(\Theta^\dagger \tilde P_i \Theta \tilde P_j\right) = \operatorname{tr}\!\left(\Theta^\dagger P_i \Theta P_j\right). \tag{83}$$

<span id="prop-69"></span>**Proposition 69 (Condition for a dynamical symmetry).** A unitary $V$ is a dynamical symmetry if and only if
$$V\,\Theta(t\leftarrow 0)\,V^\dagger = \Theta(t\leftarrow 0) \odot \left(e^{i\theta_{ij}(t)}\right) \tag{87}$$
for some phase matrix; that is, $V\Theta V^\dagger$ differs from $\Theta$ by at most a Schur–Hadamard gauge transformation (Definition 46b1). The unitary case $V\Theta V^\dagger = \Theta$ and the anti-unitary case $V\Theta V^\dagger = \overline{\Theta}$ are special cases [@barandes2025correspondence].

<span id="rem-69a"></span>**Remark 69a (Wigner's theorem).** Wigner's theorem states that any bijection of the set of pure states (Definition 24c2) of a complex Hilbert space that preserves transition probabilities $|\langle\phi,\psi\rangle|^2$ is induced by a unitary or anti-unitary operator (Definition 24e) [@wigner1959].

For a unitary symmetry generated by a self-adjoint $G$ that commutes with $U$, Noether's theorem follows as the conservation statement
$$\langle G(t) \rangle = \operatorname{tr}\!\left(G U(t\leftarrow 0)\rho(0)U^\dagger(t\leftarrow 0)\right) = \langle G(0)\rangle. \tag{93}$$

<span id="rem-69b"></span>**Remark 69b (Noether's theorem, here).** For a continuous symmetry generated by a self-adjoint $G$ commuting (Definition LA11) with the evolution, Noether's theorem here is the conservation statement $\langle G(t)\rangle=\langle G(0)\rangle$ above [@barandes2025correspondence].

Restricting to transformations that must preserve the Born rule in *every* orthonormal basis yields the stronger condition $|\tilde\Theta'_{\alpha\beta}|^2 = |\Theta'_{\alpha\beta}|^2$, whose solutions are precisely the unitary and anti-unitary operators of Wigner's theorem [@wigner1959].

## 15. Dilations, Spin, and the Complex Numbers

<span id="prop-70"></span>**Proposition 70 (Dilation as a free enlargement).** For any integer $D \ge 2$, the Hilbert-space formulation can be enlarged without changing the process by
$$\Theta \mapsto \Theta \otimes \mathbb{1}^{\mathcal{I}}, \quad P_i \mapsto P_i \otimes \mathbb{1}^{\mathcal{I}}, \quad P_j \mapsto P_j \otimes P^{\mathcal{I}}_\gamma, \tag{98}$$
where $\{P^\mathcal{I}_\gamma\}$ is a PVM on an internal space $\mathcal{H}_\mathcal{I}$ of dimension $D$. The dictionary is unchanged after a partial trace over $\mathcal{H}_\mathcal{I}$.

Dilations provide a larger "canvas" for designing transition matrices and can make new *dilation-emergeables*—such as intrinsic spin—manifest. Representing spin this way requires dilating the Hilbert space to $N D$ dimensions and introducing a $D$-dimensional representation of $SO(3)$ for the internal space, so the underlying indivisible stochastic process involves no preferred direction [@barandes2025correspondence].

<span id="rem-71"></span>**Remark 71 (Why the complex numbers appear).** Unistochastic matrices are generally *not* orthostochastic, so if the transition matrix $\Gamma$ is already unistochastic there is no guarantee that its unitary square root $U$ can be taken real orthogonal. The correspondence therefore implies that, to represent the most general indivisible stochastic processes, the complex numbers $\mathbb{C}$ are an important structural feature of quantum theory [@barandes2023theorem]. One is always free to choose $\Theta$ real, in which case the dilated $\tilde U$ is real orthogonal; and one can even double the dimension to represent the imaginary unit by a real $2\times 2$ matrix [@myrheim1999] and the complex-conjugation operator $K$ by $\sigma_x$ [@stueckelberg1960]. But even so, the algebraic structure of the complex numbers—and with it the spectral theorem, eigenvectors, anti-unitary operators, self-adjoint Hamiltonians, and the Schrödinger equation—becomes hard to avoid. These ideas are developed further in the deflationary account of [@barandes2026deflationary].

## 16. Interpretation: Measurement, Hidden Variables, Locality, and Causation

**The measurement and category problems.** In the indivisible picture, a measurement is just another stochastic interaction, modeled as one additional part of a larger stochastic process. When a measuring device is so modeled, it ends up in one of its possible outcome configurations with the standard Born-rule probability, whether the observable was a beable or an emergeable [@barandes2025correspondence]. This dissolves the measurement problem—there is no special "collapse" process, only ordinary stochastic dynamics—and addresses the category problem, since ordinary non-measurement events are the norm rather than the exception.

**Comparison with earlier stochastic reformulations.** Previous attempts to reformulate quantum theory stochastically—Bopp, Fényes, and Nelson's stochastic mechanics [@nelson1966], and later work [@aaronson2005]—assumed Markovian laws and were thus limited. Spontaneous-collapse theories instead treat the wave function as primary and literally collapsing [@ghirardi1986; @bassi2003]. Indivisible quantum theory differs from both: it is realist, has no parallel universes, and has no primitive collapse.

**Hidden variables and Bell's theorem.** The configurations of an indivisible stochastic process play the role that hidden variables played historically, but they are not hidden in the literal sense. The dynamical laws are non-Markovian, and Barandes argues that this permits locality in *space* to be preserved at the cost of **non-Markovianity**—a kind of non-locality in *time* consistent with the light-cone structure of special relativity [@barandes2025quantum]. This connects with the observation of Glick and Adami that a form of non-Markovianity is intrinsic to even closed quantum systems [@glick2020], and with earlier work on causality in EPR by Chang and Cartwright [@chang1993]. Whether this framing evades the full force of Bell's theorem [@bell1964] is developed in detail in forthcoming work; it is a central open question.

**Many-to-one, like Hamiltonian mechanics.** The correspondence is many-to-one in both directions, exactly as that between Newtonian systems and Hamiltonian mechanics. A given Hilbert space can arise from many qualitatively different configuration spaces (one per orthonormal basis), and a given process admits many Hilbert-space representations—an instance of the general underdetermination of ontology by formalism discussed by Curiel [@curiel2014].

## 17. Summary

- An **indivisible stochastic process** ([Definition 33](#def-33)) is a stochastic process whose dynamical laws consist of a single first-order transition map, defined at division events, without an infinite Kolmogorov tower.
- The free positivity of transition probabilities lets one write $\Gamma_{ij} = |\Theta_{ij}|^2$ ([Observation 44](#obs-44)), introducing the **time-evolution operator** with its Schur–Hadamard gauge freedom ([Proposition 47](#prop-47)).
- The **dictionary** $\Gamma_{ij} = \operatorname{tr}(\Theta^\dagger P_i \Theta P_j)$ ([Theorem 50](#thm-50)) translates the stochastic process into Hilbert-space language, and the law of total probability's linearity becomes the linearity of density-matrix evolution and the Born rule ([Proposition 51](#prop-51)).
- A **Kraus decomposition** ([Propositions 56–57](#prop-56)) and **Stinespring dilation** ([Theorem 59](#thm-59)) produce a unitary operator on a space of dimension at most $N^3$, whose associated transition matrix is **unistochastic**.
- The **stochastic–quantum theorem** ([Theorem 62](#thm-62)) states that every indivisible stochastic process is a subsystem of a unistochastic process, and the **stochastic–quantum correspondence** ([Corollary 64](#cor-64)) runs in both directions.
- The framework derives the Schrödinger equation, accommodates interference, decoherence, entanglement, and noncommutative observables, and reframes the measurement problem. It comes with two forms of gauge invariance, a Noether theorem, and a natural account of why complex numbers appear.

The most remarkable feature is how little is assumed. From ordinary probability, an old-fashioned configuration space, and a sparse set of first-order transition probabilities—no Hilbert space, no wave function, no unitarity postulate—one recovers the empirical content of quantum theory. Whether the residual non-Markovianity can be reconciled with relativistic locality, and whether the framework yields genuinely new predictions, are the questions that will determine its ultimate significance [@barandes2025quantum; @barandes2026deflationary].
